utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This afternoon we will have a hearing under the Rule 62 bis. The purpose of the hearing is following upon the request of the accused Sikirica and Dosen to have the Chamber determine whether it is satisfied as to the matters set out in that Rule so that it may enter a finding of guilt. If the Chamber determines that a finding of guilt is to be entered, it will set a date for the sentence hearing. I remind you of the matters in respect of which the Chamber must be satisfied. The Chamber must be satisfied that the guilty plea has been made voluntarily, that the plea is informed, that it is not equivocal, and that there is a sufficient factual basis for the crime and the accused's participation in it. The Chamber has before it the agreement entered into by the accused and the Office of the Prosecutor. I must say that in considering this matter, the Chamber attaches great significance to paragraph (e) of section D of the agreement. I think more accurately, it is paragraph 5(e), and the assertion in that paragraph that we attach particular significance to is as follows, and I read it: "Upon reflection of the parties of the evidence adduced at trial, the parties agree that the factual basis, as outlined in this plea agreement, accurately described the accused's culpability." Will the accused Sikirica stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sikirica, you have entered into a plea agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor. By this agreement, you will plead guilty to count 3 of the indictment, charging persecutions, a crime against humanity, as set out in paragraph 36(a) to (e) of the indictment, and this plea is in satisfaction of all other counts in the indictment. Have you discussed fully with your counsel the plea agreement you have made with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SIKIRICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you threatened or coerced in any way to make this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SIKIRICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have made this plea voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SIKIRICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has your counsel informed you of the nature of the charges against you and of the consequences of pleading guilty to a crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SIKIRICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he has, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pursuant to the agreement, the Prosecutor and the Defence have recommended to the Chamber that sentence fall within the range of 10 and 17 years. You must understand, however, that the sentence will ultimately be determined by the Chamber in accordance with the Statute and the Rules. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SIKIRICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SIKIRICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sikirica, stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How do you plead to count 3 of the indictment, charging you with persecutions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SIKIRICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I plead guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber, having heard all the submissions, and in particular having examined the joint submissions by the parties, is satisfied that the plea was made voluntarily, that it was informed, not equivocal, and that there is a sufficient factual basis for the crime and of the accused's participation in it. Accordingly, the Chamber enters a finding of guilt. Mr. Ryneveld? Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The plea having been accepted by the Chamber, according to the agreement, the Prosecutor withdraws -- will withdraw all the other charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And in light of the Chamber's decision, the Prosecutor will withdraw or has withdrawn the additional charges against the accused Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will consider the date for the sentence hearing after we have dealt with the other matter. Will the accused Dosen stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You entered into a plea agreement with the Prosecutor whereby you will plead guilty to count 3 of the indictment, charging persecution, as set out in paragraph 36(b), (d) and (e) of the indictment, and this plea will be in satisfaction of all the other counts in the indictment. Now, have you discussed fully with your counsel the plea agreement you have made with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED DOSEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you threatened or coerced in any way to make this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED DOSEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And has your counsel informed you of the nature of the charges against you and of the consequences of pleading guilty to a crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED DOSEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he has, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pursuant to the agreement, the Prosecutor and the Defence have recommended to the Chamber that sentence fall within the range of five and seven years, but you must understand that the sentence will ultimately be determined by the Chamber in accordance with the Statute and the Rules. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED DOSEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How do you plead to count 3 of the indictment, charging you with persecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED DOSEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I plead guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sit. You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber, having heard the submissions, is satisfied that the plea was made voluntarily, that it was informed, not equivocal, and that there is a sufficient factual basis for the crime and of the accused's participation in it. Accordingly, the Chamber enters a finding of guilt. Mr. Mundis, or Ms. Baly, I'm sorry, the Chamber having accepted the plea in accordance with the agreement, the Prosecutor will withdraw the other charges?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we turn now to the date for the sentence hearing? You will recall that on Monday, the 8th and Tuesday, the 9th of October, we will be hearing submissions in respect of the accused Kolundzija. The Chamber will fix Wednesday, the 10th and Thursday, the 11th for the sentence hearing in respect of Sikirica and Dosen. Mr. Greaves, you've already indicated that you will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I hope I always try to be in these cases, yes. I anticipate that a short written submission can be made in respect of these matters. I would anticipate actually being no more than an hour at the very most in oral submissions before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think I'm being long. I would hope to keep it shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic? What is your estimate of the time that you will need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, between 45 minutes and one hour will, I'm sure, be sufficient, in addition to what we submit in our written submission. So I think we will be able to comply with the schedule we have just heard from you here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There was one matter I omitted to mention in relation to scheduling. Could we also adhere, then, to the date for filing of briefs, which I think is October the 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be on the Monday, the 1st. The sentencing briefs should be filed by Monday, the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is one other matter that I need to remind the system of. A report is to be prepared by Mr. McFadden, the commandant of the United Nations Detention Unit, If I can just gently remind the system that that needs to be prepared and ready for the sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm informed that the report will be transmitted to the Registry this afternoon. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sir Ivan? Sorry, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I would just like confirmation for your part whether the dates relate to the accused Mr. Dosen with respect to the final sentencing brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. To all three, yes. Sir Ivan, you did give us an estimate of the time that you would need, but I just ask you to repeat it, because we have you down for two days. Will you need two days? Because if you don't, then we could make an adjustment in respect of the other hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm bound to say that we haven't yet been able to ascertain precisely what witnesses will be available, what witnesses we need to call, what witnesses we can serve by way of statement. But there is the question of the medical witness, and at the moment I haven't up-to-date news about how that is progressing. I think it's safer to keep to the original plan, that we should be able to complete our task in the two days allotted. If it should go a little short, then perhaps that can't be helped. If I know in sufficient advance -- and I will be with my learned junior who is handling all these matters next week. He has been unable to come today. Firstly, we didn't think it would be necessary; and secondly, sad things have happened which make it very difficult for him to fly out of Chicago, in any event. But we will be getting together over the next few days, and I may be able to provide the Court with more up-to-date information. If that should -- information should be usable for the purposes of speeding things, then I'm sure all of us might agree that we might arrange that, but I think it's safer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll stick to the two days. And if you can let us know in sufficient time to make the adjustment, then that would be very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: There are just two matters which, since I'm on my feet, I would be grateful for the Chamber's guidance on. Firstly, it would be helpful if we had the governor of the Detention Centre's report before we finalised our written brief. I know that there's been an indication that it should be available today or tomorrow, but I'm afraid that sometimes things go adrift, and I would like to be assured that even if it can't be available today or tomorrow, it will be available sometime next week so that we can close that with our final brief. That's the first point. The second is: I wonder if the Court could give a ruling on the length of the written brief. I have looked with care and even sought advice about the meaning of the practice direction on the length of briefs, which does not specifically address the length of a written brief where a plea of not guilty has turned into a plea of guilty, particularly before any evidence has been called for the Defence. And on the one hand, it says that final trial briefs - which in a sense this is - should not exceed 200 pages or 60.000 words; on the other hand, other motions - which this may not be - replies and responses, which this certainly isn't, are not to exceed 10 pages or 3.000 words. So somewhere there, there is -- there must be some indication of whether we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you should just give us an indication as to how long you think your brief will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In excess of 10 pages, certainly. It also depends upon whether enclosed in the written brief are the references in quotations, which make it much easier for the Chamber to read, or whether it's got to be done by footnotes and annexes, which makes it more difficult for the Chamber to read. Obviously, the latter will considerably increase the length of the final brief; the former will shorten it. But even foreshortened, I couldn't do it in ten pages whilst doing justice to Kolundzija's case, bearing in mind in this that he hasn't yet presented his defence or any of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would it exceed 15 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Well, at the moment it does. I can give an undertaking to the Court that it will be as short as possible, but the Court might think it helpful for the future to give some kind of indication as to how it reads, section 4 and section 5, in relation to this matter, so that it doesn't have to be raised, as it were, on the floor of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll leave it to your judgement to present a brief as short --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Precisely, as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I will do it. I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are there any other matters? Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly to follow up with what counsel for the accused Kolundzija had said, the Prosecution is intending, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, to file one consolidated sentencing brief with respect to all three of these individuals, primarily because the camp conditions section, which we are intending on pointing out, will be similar for all three of them. I would not expect our sentencing brief to exceed 30 to 35 pages in total with respect to all three individuals, and I would first like a clarification that that would be acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it would be. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then finally, with respect to actual arguments with respect to the three individuals before you, the Prosecution also is intending on providing oral submissions with respect again to the camp conditions, which would be relevant and probative, in our view, to the sentences of all three of the individuals. Under the scenario that the Trial Chamber has outlined for us this afternoon, what we would envision, or at least our understanding from what you've directed today, would be that Mr. Kolundzija would present his case on Monday and Tuesday, the 8th and 9th, and then would immediately move into sentencing arguments with respect to Mr. Kolundzija. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution then would simply like to alert the Chamber or request clarification from the Chamber that it would be permissible for the Prosecution at that time to develop its oral arguments with respect to camp conditions, which would also be relevant to the other two accused when we present specific sentencing arguments with respect to those two individuals on the following two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be permissible. That means that counsel for the other accused should be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I wonder if the Court would bear with me for a moment. In response to what Mr. Mundis has said, with respect, it would be very helpful - I'm not sure that we wouldn't be entitled - to have the Prosecution's written brief before we submit our own written briefs. Certainly it would be helpful in as much as we could tailor our responses to any of the arguments which are adduced by the Prosecution in our written brief, provided we had it in advance. Well, that doesn't give them a great deal of time. Our briefs have got to be in by the 1st of October, so they've effectively only got next week and the week after. If we could have some kind of assurance that their brief will be provided to us in good time, then I shall be content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would be prepared to submit its sentencing brief on Friday -- I believe it's the 27th, 28th of September. I believe October 1st is a Monday, if I'm not mistaken. We would be prepared to submit our brief on the Friday prior to that Monday, if that would be of assistance to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm afraid it wouldn't be of much assistance to the Defence, because in order for ours to be served by the 1st of October, I have in mind that it should be present for printing and whatever is required by the weekend of the 28th of September. By that time, of course, if what Mr. Mundis has said is going to be accurate, then we won't have known and we won't have been able to respond to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, can you get yours in by the Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would respectfully request that rather than moving the date of our submission up, if perhaps the date that the Defence could file their sentencing briefs be pushed back the other direction. In other words, perhaps rather than theirs being due on the 1st of October, perhaps their responses could be due on Wednesday, the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, and I see that my learned friends also agree. That would be helpful to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, then. The Defence sentence brief by Wednesday, the 3rd of October. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: adjourned at 3.12 p.m. 25
